summary:
Benin does not criminalise same-sex relations anywhere in its territory. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that alongside this legality, discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics is not prohibited by law, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. The statutory position is therefore legal but entirely unshielded: a trans visitor has no recognition pathway to rely on and no statutory protection to invoke.

The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices found that Benin's law does not explicitly prohibit SOGIESC discrimination and that LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised. The report describes hostility toward the community as most pronounced outside major urban areas, and records LGBTQI+ persons being routinely refused medical care, hormone treatment among the services named, as well as social services. A trans visitor who depends on continued hormone supply or on any form of public or contracted care should treat that denial as documented rather than hypothetical, and should weigh the urban/rural split when choosing where to stay and seek treatment.

Physical risk is documented at a level well above statutory exposure. An Erasing 76 Crimes report of 9 April 2024 states that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin. The same report describes the Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre, operating since about 2020 as a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the wider sub-region have passed. That infrastructure is small relative to the scale of violence described, and it is survivor-support rather than a protection mechanism a visitor can plan around.

Religious institutions form part of the hostility pattern. A Washington Blade feature of 31 August 2015, commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups, reported LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describing discrimination and persecution from both their churches and their governments. The account dates from 2015 and serves as context for the institutional environment rather than as current-state evidence.
tangentialFactors:
Benin's position sits within a West African regional pattern in which statutory non-criminalisation does not translate into protection. The 2015 Washington Blade account places Benin alongside Ghana, Togo and Nigeria in describing religious-institution hostility, while Outright International's 2026 overview places it among jurisdictions where SOGIESC discrimination goes unaddressed in law.

The gap between law and enforcement is the central turbulence factor. Same-sex relations are legal, yet the 2023 US country report documents refusal of medical care and social services and heightened hostility outside major urban areas, and the 2024 Erasing 76 Crimes report describes anti-gay lynchings as commonplace. Formal legality therefore offers a visitor little practical cover, particularly outside Cotonou and Porto-Novo.

Legal gender recognition being impossible has a direct practical edge at borders and in hotels: a trans visitor's passport or identity documents cannot be aligned with their presentation through any Beninese procedure, so any mismatch between documents and presentation is a matter for the traveller's own document strategy rather than for local recognition.
localsOnly:
Benin's statutory legality sits on a deep historical baseline rather than on recent liberalisation. Anthropologist Patrick Awondo, of political sociology and medical anthropology at EHESS Paris, has cited evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits recorded women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom, whose territory is modern Benin. Same-sex practice in the country is thus indigenous in origin rather than a colonial import, a framing that shapes how local advocates argue the case.

Registration is closed to LGBTI organisations under the current framework described by Outright International as of March 2026, which constrains how residents can organise, fundraise and publicise. The Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre has operated since about 2020 with 20 places, and almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed through it, indicating demand far exceeding capacity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa rules for trans visitors, including any document or marker requirements at Cotonou's airport, are not addressed anywhere in the source inventory and remain unresolved here.

The inventory contains no material on hate-crime legislation, on whether the lynchings described have produced prosecutions, or on the enforcement record for the medical-care refusals noted in the 2023 US report. Those questions are unresolved rather than answered in the negative.

The claims that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace and that almost 380 young people have passed through a single 20-place centre come from an advocacy publication and a 2015 commissioned feature respectively; neither figure is corroborated by an official or statistical source in this inventory.
